en: The Secret Ritual Manual for the Practice of the Bodhisattva Mahā-Vairocana Tathāgata,
the Great Holy Hevajra, the Deity of Joy,
in His Union of Equalized Samādhi and Prajñā.
Translated by the Imperial Preceptor of Honglu, the Great Master of Vast Wisdom Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree:
If there are disciples of the Buddha—namely, the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—
If good sons or good daughters and others wish to practice this Dharma of the Holy Celestial Bodhisattva,
so that their requests and aspirations may be accomplished according to their hearts' desires, [they should proceed as follows].
First, one must offer all precious treasures to the laborers, the Dharma Master, and the Ācārya,
providing them with food and drink of a hundred flavors in order to cause them to attain a joyful heart.
Requisites and wealth,
clothing and seats,
as well as personal belongings.
After making offerings and causing [the recipient] to attain a joyful mind,
one should inquire about and thoroughly study the subtle, secret, and ultimate meaning of the essential principles.
One should practice the secret Dharma.
Regarding the essential methods for achieving accomplishment, one must wondrously sacrifice the body to seek the Way and exhaust all precious treasures in diligent labor.
This refers to clothing for sustaining the body and food and drink for prolonging life; that is to say,
the materials by which one's own person may be clothed.
One may personally consume food and drink as provisions to make offerings to the Dharma-transmitting Master and the Dharma-knowing Ācārya;
one should offer these until all rare treasures are exhausted through diligent labor.
First, one must warm one *śroṇa* of sesame oil over a fire;
then, empower the charcoal, the vessel, the fire-net,
and the white copper *tāla* by reciting the Great Mantra one hundred and eight times.
Furthermore, perform the warming and the empowerment;
the mudrā is simply that of the three-pronged spear.
The Root Great Mantra is as follows: [The Body Mantra].
*Namo vainayikā-hāsita-mukha-jātī-ta | Oṃ vainayika vainayika vinayaka vinayaka trāyaka paritrāyaka saṃkhāhāsita-saṃkha-kiccha-śānti-kara svāhā.* Recite this three times during the midday ablution.
On ordinary days, perform four invocations at dawn;
continue the ritual ablutions for a period of seven days to seek the attainment of *siddhi*.
Consecrate the offerings with a few recitations of the heart-mantra.
These offerings— such as lotus roots, *modaka* cakes, seasonal fruits, and so forth—
are presented solely for the worship of the manifest deities and sages.
Within seven days, the result will surely be verified.
The mantra for the minor rite is:
Oṃ jili-kṣve sa-bha-ha (dissolve the two syllables), followed by the completion of the offering and presentation.
Recite the verse of praise:

Oṃ gaṇapati tustaye svāhā mahāgaṇapataye tustaye karāya svāhā. This is for the sake of accomplishing all that is sought and desired, so that they may be fulfilled and perfected according to one's wishes.
One should cause the Dharma-transmitting Ācārya to rejoice;
thereafter, one may practice for seven days and attain the four kinds of siddhi.
Breathing, increasing, loving, and harmonizing—
these are called the four methods for accomplishing *siddhi*.
Thus it is stated in the *Vinaya-sūtra*.
That is to say, when this noble Bodhisattva makes offerings and presents [them],
there are three kinds of karmic fruits.
First is the superior grade of offering and presentation.
May those who offer middling-grade worship attain the majestic power of a king;
may those who offer inferior-grade worship become wealthy, possessing the seven treasures.
Food and clothing will not be lacking; they will be naturally provided in abundance and full measure.
Those who offer the highest grade of offerings shall cause the Dharma-transmitting person to attain a heart of joy.
The secret and profound essential meaning has been bestowed as instruction.
Regarding the offering according to the Dharma:

while the ritual for the middle-grade offering can be seen in other sources, here we present the concise offering according to the essential path of the sequence for those who have not yet realized it.
As for those who offer the lower grade of service,
they do not bathe him with oil; rather,
he is simply invited to sit in a separate hall.
Whatever is obtained, one should first offer a portion as an act of worship;
this is called the inferior grade [of practice] for the Buddha’s disciples in the final age.
If one harbors within one's own mind a heart of stinginess, greed, pride, and attachment,
one will not achieve the state of an Ācārya who transmits the Dharma and knows the Way, nor will one attain a heart of joy, delight, and congratulation.
While they do not inquire into the profound intent of the detailed instructions nor seek realization,
they nonetheless receive coarse and superficial offerings and practice;
yet they slander the profound, secret, and supreme path.
It draws in the seeds of poverty and lack of merit.
The *Tiantai Zhizhe Ajari Shikan Shin'yōki* (Record of the Essentials of the Mind of Calming and Contemplation by the Tiantai Master Zhizhe) states:
"That is to say, there is merit but no wisdom."
"This fool is no different from a dragon-bodied ghost," and so forth; "he possesses wisdom but lacks merit.
This person of perverse delusion does not possess the mind of a sage or a noble one.
In this world, there are none who lack merit;
indeed, among those who practice in the world, there are none whose merit does not adorn them.
This is because when the holy Bodhisattva Deva made offerings and practiced his cultivation, [he was thus adorned].
One must certainly bring to perfection both merit and wisdom.
Concentration is merit;
wisdom is the equanimity of the three samādhis.
This teaching has two periods,
one at dawn and the other at midday.
These two times—the dawn and the period of increase—are auspicious;
midday is also a time of auspiciousness.
This is why one should offer worship to this noble deity at these times.
"Only those who are fully endowed with the perfection of merit and wisdom [hear this].
Furthermore, regarding those people who follow the provisional teachings within the Vinaya school, there will be no equality for a hundred generations, and so forth.
This dharma uses wine as an offering for *fuzi* (aconite)."
This poisonous substance, when obtained by a physician, becomes a medicine that cures disease and brings peace to the body;
when blended by a skilled compounding master,
it becomes *yogha*, this wine, a water of joy and a sublime elixir.
This wine pleases even the farmer;
it can turn what is drunk by people into medicine.
For those who habitually drink poison,
this causes them to become ill; however, because it brings joy to the hearts of these devas and bodhisattvas,
they offer wine as an oblation— this is merely called "water of joy."
If one makes offerings and serves the current king or noble lord at the proper time,
one will certainly obtain spiritual efficacy.
There is no fault in consuming the remnants offered to the mantra-reciter;
this is prescribed by the Dharma.
This particular rite, however, has no such prescription.
In this age of the final dharma, disciples of the Buddha should give rise to a sincere heart of faith and resolve;
with utmost sincerity and earnest devotion, they should offer worship and service,
never allowing doubt to arise.
The transmitter of the Dharma asks those who know the Dharma to seek full training, realization, faith, and practice;
it must not be treated with negligence.
Regarding the sequential methods, the *ācārya*’s inclusion of the full ordination (*upasampadā*) is not recorded [here].
The ritual manual (vidhi) text enables one to sequentially receive, study, awaken to, make offerings to, practice, believe in, and uphold the Dharma with great joy.
This is the original text from Tōji. Recorded by Shunshō in the Kan’ei era. Shun.
Once finished.
